steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Context: the social, cultural, historical and political circumstances in which a play was written AND in which it is performed.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Original context shapes the play's meaning — An Inspector Calls (1945, set 1912) uses dramatic irony about world wars the audience knew had happened.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Modern production context: a director may reset a play in a different period to make contemporary connections — this changes the meaning.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Social influences: class, gender, race, power structures — these are reflected in and critiqued by drama.

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Why is it important to understand the social and historical context of a play when analysing it? | How might a modern production of a classic play change the meaning through its context? Give an example. | Explain how the original performance context of a play you have studied affects its meaning.

steps.title: Check your answers
steps.body: Context reveals the playwright's intentions — they wrote for a specific audience with specific concerns. Without context, you miss the social commentary, the political critique and the historical refe | A modern production might reset the play in a contemporary context — e.g. setting The Crucible during modern 'cancel culture' rather than the McCarthy era. The story is the same but the context shifts | Specific example: e.g. Blood Brothers (1983) was written during Thatcher's Britain when class divisions were deepening — the musical's theme of class determining fate reflects this specific political

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Always consider BOTH the original context AND the production's context Context is not background — it SHAPES meaning Use context to explain WHY the playwright made specific choices Modern productions may deliberately change context — analyse WHY
